Melkoṭe
------------------------------------------
Places of पिल्ग्रिमगे have played a very important role in preserving and reforming Hindu religion and culture. If some places have acquired importance due to the location of famous temples, and, others due to the association with great saints, मेल्कोटे, a small town in the Mandya district of Karnataka State of South India, has the distinction of both. The ancient temple of Nārāyaṇasvāmi and the intimate association with Rāmānuja (A.

-1137) the doyen among the teachers and propagators of the Viśiṣṭā-द्वैत Vedānta school, over a period of twelve years have made this little sleepy town, one of the four chief fortresses of the cult of श्रीवैष्णविस्म्.
Situated 48 kms. north-west of Mysore and 157 kms. south-west of Bangalore—the capital of Karnataka—the मेल्कोटे town is perched on a small hillock of pink granite, that rises about 150 metres above the surrounding plains. It has a salubrious climate and agriculture is the main occupation of the residents.
Known variously, over the centuries, as Melgoṭe, Yādavagiri, Tirunārāyaṇa-puram, भूलोक-वैकुण्ठ and Dakṣiṇa-बदरिकाश्रम, its political control had changed hands several times due to the vicissitudes of history. The Gaṅgas (8th century), the Coḷas (10th and 11th centuries) and the Hoysaḷas (12th century) were the main dynasties that ruled over मेल्कोटे before Rāmānuja’s arrival. Rulers of Vijayanagara empire and the Woḍeyars of Mysore controlled it in later times.
It was during the rule of विष्णु-vardhana (A.

-1142) of Hoysaḷa dynasty that Rāmānuja arrived at मेल्कोटे incognito from श्रीरङ्गम् (now in Tamil Nadu) to escape from persecution at the hands of the Śaiva rulers there. Sometime during this period of his stay at मेल्कोटे (A.

-1128) he renovated the ancient Nārāyaṇasvāmi temple with the king’s help and reorganized its rituals and management. Over the years this temple town has grown into an influential seat of the cult of श्रीवैष्णविस्म् with several temples and maṭhas (traditional monasteries) accruing to it.
Apart from the Nārāyaṇasvāmi temple complex, the only other major temple is that of नरसिṁह (‘Man-lion’ इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु) situated on the top of the hillock adjoining the Kalyāṇī or temple-tank. There are, of course, several minor but independent shrines outside the temple-complex. Shrines dedicated to Veṅkaṭaramaṇa (an aspect of विष्णु as found in तिरुपति), Varāha (‘Boar-इन्चर्नतिओन्’ of विष्णु) and राम are near the Kalyāṇī. Two shrines—one of गणपति and another of Kālī—are situated in two different corners, a little away from habitation.
Apart from these temples and shrines, there are also four maṭhas or monasteries well-known in the annals of the history of श्रीवैष्णविस्म्: अहोबिल मठ, परकाल मठ, Vānamāmalai मठ and Yatirāja मठ.
The Nārāyaṇasvāmi temple—also called Celuvarāyasvāmi temple in the local language—is the most sacred and important structure situated at the southern end of the flat plateau occupied by the present town. It is rectangular in plan (75 x 60 metres) and faces east. The गर्भगृह (cella) and the ardhamaṇḍapa (passage-hall) are the oldest part of the structure built probably during the early part of the 11th century. Additional structures like pradakṣiṇā (passage for circumambulation) and pillared corridors or halls have been continually added right up to the early part of the 19th century.
Apart from the shrine for the main deity नारायण, there are subsidiary shrines for the देवी (known as ‘Tāyār’ or मोथेर् and ‘Yadugiri Nacciyar’), the procession image known as ‘Śelvapiḷḷai’, Rāmānuja and a few other saints.
The gopuram or tower over the main entrance is imposing.
Out of the several annual festivals of this temple the ब्रह्मोत्सव conducted during March-April is the biggest. It is spread over twelve days. Since the deity is adorned with the ‘Vairamuḍi’ (a huge diamond crown of unknown antiquity) on the night of the sixth day, the festival is also called ‘Vairamuḍi उत्सव’. This attracts a very huge gathering every year.
The only other temple of almost equal importance in मेल्कोटे is the नरसिṁह-svāmi temple located at the highest peak of the eastern fringe of the hill. There is a flight of steps leading to it. Half-way up, two rock-cut caves are also seen.
There is a Sanskrit school (pāṭhaśālā) attached to the main temple. In the recent times a big institute has come up in the town for encouraging studies in Viśiṣṭā-द्वैत Vedānta as also research.
See also RĀMĀNUJA, ŚRĪVAIṢṆAVISAM and VAIRAMUḌI.
